artworks.title: Caeneus and the Centaur (Attic black-figure)
artworks.description: Louvre CA 2494: the invulnerable Lapith Caeneus (Kaineus) is driven into the earth by a centaur — the death Ovid later retells, when spears fail and the Centaurs bury him under trees and stones. One of the clearest archaic images of the figure.

artworks.title: Caeneus Group (detail of the François Vase)
artworks.description: Detail from the François Vase (Florence): the Caeneus group within the centauromachy frieze, naming the Lapith among the warriors at Peirithous' wedding — archaic testimony that Caeneus already belonged to the feast that becomes a battle.

artworks.title: Centaurs Fighting Caeneus (Lycian sarcophagus, Istanbul)
artworks.description: Short side of the Lycian sarcophagus in the Istanbul Archaeological Museum: two centaurs hammer the invulnerable Caeneus into the ground — the same burial-death Greek art reserved for the Lapith who could not be pierced.

artworks.title: Centaurs and Caeneus (bronze relief, Olympia)
artworks.description: A small bronze relief in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia: centaurs overwhelm Caeneus — portable testimony to the Lapith's distinctive death in the centauromachy.

popCulture.title: Metamorphoses
popCulture.creator: Ovid
popCulture.description: Nestor's inset tale: Caenis becomes invulnerable Caeneus and is crushed by centaurs under a pile of trees — Ovid's gender change at the Lapith wedding.

popCulture.title: Caeneus
popCulture.description: The Lapith transformed from Caenis — unpierceable warrior, buried alive, a figure modern reception keeps for the metamorphosis itself.

popCulture.title: Lapiths
popCulture.description: Caeneus' people at Peirithous' feast — the centauromachy that ends the invulnerable man's career.
